text: Binary search takes log₂ n steps. What does information theory add to that fact?
choices: It explains why the base of the logarithm matters, since bits are base 2.
Each comparison yields at most one bit, and identifying one of n items requires log₂ n bits — so the complexity bound and the information bound are the same bound.
It shows the bound can be beaten if the comparisons are chosen adaptively.
It proves binary search is optimal only for uniformly distributed keys.
explanation: The information in a message is the number of well-chosen yes-or-no questions needed to determine it. Guessing a number from 1 to 1000 takes about 10 questions, and log₂ 1000 ≈ 9.97. A limit on how fast an algorithm can run turns out to be a limit on how fast information can be gathered — the same connection underlies Chapter 32's comparison-sort lower bound.
